https://mymotherlode.com/entertainment/1.text: 74.3 ° F Full Weather | Burn Info Sponsored By: Movie stars, timely documentaries and awards hopefuls convene at the Venice Film Festival Add us as a preferred source By AP News Published Aug 29, 2026 11:37 pm Venice Film Festival-Preview View Photos August can be a dreary month for Hollywood glamour, but the Venice Film Festival is on the horizon to kick off the busy fall film festival season in style. There will be plenty of stars gracing the red carpets when the 83rd edition of the festival kicks off Wednesday on the Lido: Noel and Liam Gallagher, Robert Pattinson, Rooney Mara, George Clooney and Penélope Cruz are among those expected to attend. Some of the films may even become Oscar nominees. But the mood feels a little different this year. There will always be a spotlight for the Hollywood contingent and the awards hopefuls posing on boats and docks in designer duds. Yet, in a lineup featuring Pattinson as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen, Dakota Johnson as Marilyn Monroe, Guy Pearce as Rupert Murdoch and Clooney as, well, himself (he’s getting a lifetime achievement award, as is Ellen Burstyn), it’s possible that much of the attention will be on a man who (probably) won’t be there: Elon Musk. Docs feature Musk, Russia and Gaza Alex Gibney’s nearly four-hour documentary about the world’s richest man has been in the works for almost four years. The Oscar-winner wasn’t sure about taking it on at first, but a good friend convinced him it would be a worthy portrait of 21st-century power — and this was before the 2024 presidential campaign and DOGE. When the documentary was announced, Musk called it a “hit piece” on social media. Gibney replied, “How would you know?” In fact, Gibney told The Associated Press he started off as a kind of admirer — as well as a Tesla owner — and sincerely wanted to talk to Musk for the film. “Ultimately, he didn’t want to talk to me,” Gibney said. “But then you start, you know, digging into the facts and you follow them where they lead. And where they led, for me, was to a place that upended the myth, I would say, of Elon Musk as a kind of modern Leonardo da Vinci … I think that the news in this film is that Musk isn’t an inventor. He’s a confidence man.” The filmmakers talked to hundreds of people on and off the record to compile a sweeping picture of the Tesla and SpaceX CEO who, Gibney said, is not dissimilar to the guys at Enron or Elizabeth Holmes. He was most surprised by how many people seemed to be afraid to be on camera talking about Musk — even his admirers wanted permission first. “I thought, wow, for such a big and powerful person, that seems awfully weak,” Gibney said. But while it’s a “dark and dangerous topic,” Gibney said, the film is also a “fun ride.” The same could be said of “My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile,” in which Julia Loktev continues her sprawling portrait of independent Russian journalists after the invasion of Ukraine. “You see this group of young, very young journalists who’ve just fled their country, like, on a few hours’ notice. They had the choice of, you know, stop reporting the truth about the war, which didn’t seem like a choice at all, or go to prison, or leave the country so they can keep telling the truth,” Loktev said. “It was a question of how long do you keep following? Because this takes place over four years. And over that time, exile becomes, of course, indefinite.” Similar to the first film, Part II runs nearly six hours. But, she said, “I hear it goes by easy.” The conflict in Gaza will also take center stage in the documentary “NAZA,” a late addition to the competition, from two of the filmmakers behind the Oscar-winning “No Other Land.” Unlike last year, no large-scale protests are planned, but the group Venice4Palestine did call on the festival to “suspend all agreements with entities and institutions linked to the Israeli government.” It also asked that the Palestinian flag be flown throughout. Hollywood eyes awards in Venice Part of the intrigue of Venice is how it might play into the Oscar race — it’s usually good for a best picture nominee or two. Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine,” starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as 1970s CIA agents, seems like a promising candidate after his last two films debuted at Venice and went on to nominations. “The Father” filmmaker Florian Zeller returns with “Bunker,” a psychological thriller with Cruz and Javier Bardem. Danny Boyle looks at a turning point in tabloid media in “Ink.” And there’s much curiosity around Lance Oppenheim’s “Primetime,” for Pattinson’s performance and for its examination of reality television culture in the early 2000s. Japanese filmmaker Hirokazu Kore-eda is also debuting “Look Back,” about two small-town girls who aspire to be manga artists. And Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong examines themes of labor and freedom through two married couples in “Possible Love.” This is also a year in which big Hollywood hasn’t needed the sheen of the international film festival. Cannes was bereft of a big blockbuster, and the industry went on to have one of its highest-earning summers ever. The reigning best picture winner, “One Battle After Another,” skipped festivals entirely. Venice might have more Hollywood films than Cannes did, but following several years in which fates might have been prematurely decided for both would-be contenders, like “After the Hunt” and “The Smashing Machine,” and blockbusters like “Joker: Folie à Deux,” it too seems a bit more muted — at least on paper. Venice fails in its pledge to women And then there is the subject of women, specifically those behind the camera. There is only one in the main competition: Danish-Egyptian director May El-Toukhy. The same thing happened in 2018, prompting the festival that year to sign a pledge to have at least half of the films in competition be directed by women by 2020, which they have yet to achieve. Adding more insult to injury is the fact that Maggie Gyllenhaal, whose first film “The Lost Daughter” won Venice’s best screenplay prize in 2021, is presiding over a jury which includes Kaouther Ben Hania, whose film “The Voice of Hind Rajab” won the Silver Lion last year when there were six female-directed films in the competition. Only seven women have won the Golden Lion, including Laura Poitras with “All the Beauty and the Bloodshed,” who is returning this year with a short film she co-directed with Rachel Lauren Mueller about U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Minneapolis. “They’re Here” is part of the Venice Open section, which also includes Gyllenhaal’s Marilyn Monroe short “Flesh Impact.” Outside of the main competition, there are also documentaries from Loktev, Barbara Kopple and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi. There are several others in the Horizons sections as well, including a short from Saoirse Ronan. Opening Venice Days on Wednesday is Hungarian filmmaker Lili Horvát’s English-language debut, “My Notes on Mars,” about a couple — Rupert Friend and Mackenzie Davis — whose marriage is in trouble when the wife, a scientist, mysteriously disappears and then reappears the day of her memorial service. “The story argues for great love,” Horvát said. “Yet it shows the eternal limits of knowing the person we are in love with.” Venice Days is an independent sidebar in which more than half the selections are by women, including several high-profile shorts from filmmakers like Mona Fastvold and Claire Denis. “It’s good to be in a progressive section,” Horvát said. ___ For more coverage of the 2026 Venice Film Festival, visit: https://apnews.com/hub/venice-film-festival By LINDSEY BAHR AP Film Writer Other Entertainment News ‘Practical Magic 2’ conjures a No. 1 box office debut with $30 million Celine Dion thrills fans with emotional comeback concert after overcoming rare illness Today in History: September 13, Rabin and Arafat sign Oslo Accord Today in History: September 12, Voyager 1 leaves the solar system ‘Woman Unknown’ wins Golden Lion, Malkovich ‘humbled’ by best actor award at Venice Film Festival What’s happening at TIFF: ‘I Play Rocky scores a knockout, and a victory lap for ‘Obsession’ At the Venice Film Festival, grappling with the state of the world and crying with Oasis Make Us Your Home Page Today Events 13 Sun 14 Mon 15 Tue 16 Wed 17 Thu Cal Alumni Burgers at the Lair Lair of the Golden Bear | 12:00 am - http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27930.text: Big News Network.com Nearly 40 pct of Slovak households dissatisfied with living standards: survey BRATISLAVA, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Nearly 40 percent of Slovak households feel they are not living a decent life, with income and financial security playing a major role in how they assess their living standards, the News Agency of the Slovak Republic reported on Saturday. The report cited a June survey conducted by the research company Focus for the Partners Foundation, which found that 39 percent of households said they were not living a decent life. Respondents associated a decent standard of living primarily with adequate housing, quality food, the ability to cover regular expenses and having savings for unexpected costs. "The issue is not about affording a luxurious life. They assess whether they can manage their everyday expenses and look to the future without fear," said sociologist Martin Slosiarik with Focus. According to the survey, Slovak households estimated that they would need an average monthly income of 2,720 euros (3156.18 U.S. dollars) to maintain a decent standard of living. Almost half of households, however, said that a monthly income of up to 2,200 euros (2552.80 dollars) would be sufficient. Financial pressure on households has also increased. Some 87 percent of respondents said that government consolidation measures had affected their family budgets, while more than one-third reported that their financial situation had deteriorated over the past 12 months. The survey also showed that Slovak households' financial reserves have fallen to a 10-year low. Almost one-quarter of households had no savings, while only 14 percent had reserves sufficient to cover at least six months. Photograph: Michael Kappeler/DPA/AP Espionage ‘Stab to the heart’: arrest of German ex-spymaster sparks calls for reform Claims that August Hanning exploited intelligence for private clients comes after other troubling espionage scandals Deborah Cole in Berlin Sun 11 Oct 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he ex-spymaster August Hanning once criticised Germany’s own intelligence services as “vegetarians” among prowling carnivores, demanding broader powers to keep the country safe in a treacherous world. Often described as a “godfather” of Germany’s 21st-century security architecture, Hanning is now charged with treasonous espionage and handing state secrets to a foreign power in one of the most spectacular alleged intelligence breaches of the postwar period. If true, Hanning may have irreparably damaged Germany’s global security cooperation while exposing grievous internal vulnerabilities, in a tale ripped from a far-fetched political thriller. “This is an incident that has the potential to escalate into a genuine national scandal,” said Konstantin von Notz, a Bundestag member who sits on the parliamentary intelligence supervisory committee. Von Notz warned of a “devastating” loss of trust among partner countries “whose support we cannot do without in the current extremely tense security situation”. Tuesday’s scenes from a small town in Germany staggered even seasoned spy watchers: masked commandos led Hanning from his estate in his birthplace, Nordwalde, to a black police van, his familiar bespectacled face framed by neatly combed white hair. His expression was calm and focused, his wrists without handcuffs. View image in fullscreen Masked commandos led Hanning from his estate in Nordwalde to a police van. Photograph: Christoph Reichwein/DPA/AP The detention of the 80-year-old, who ran the federal foreign intelligence service (BND) from 1998 to 2005, marked a first in a western democracy given his previous rank, according to experts. Federal prosecutors believe Hanning ran his former chief of staff, identified only as Manfred D, as a mole at the BND, paying him to spirit out nearly 2,000 documents, at least some of them classified, over 12 years. He then allegedly exploited the intelligence for clients of the private consulting firm he launched after retiring – a legal business model that drew fierce criticism over the course of a tumultuous week. Hanning is in pretrial detention and has, through his lawyers, denied passing on confidential documents to foreign powers. If convicted, he could face 10 years in prison. Many of the compromised files are believed to have been briefing papers prepared for top officials including the chancellor. The former BND vice-president Arndt Freytag von Loringhoven described the material as the “crown jewels of the BND”, telling Der Spiegel magazine they were “the most important assessments that a BND president provides”. The explosive case sent allied secret services scrambling to assess the possible damage. A western official told Reuters that US foreign intelligence was included in documents stolen from the BND. The CIA has not commented on the case. Luca Manns, managing director of the Intelligence Services Research Unit at the University of Cologne, called the case a “stab to the heart” of the BND, causing incalculable damage to allied cooperation. “It won’t be an abrupt break,” Manns said, predicting a “creeping erosion of partnerships”. View image in fullscreen Hanning is in pretrial detention and, if convicted, could face 10 years in prison. Photograph: Anna Szilágyi/EPA The suspected betrayal could be corrosive within the agencies as well as in public perception, said Dieter Bacher, a historian at the University of Graz in Austria specialising in secret services. “When the former head of a service does something like this, the implications are, of course, enormous,” he said. “A loss of trust is certainly inevitable. As information from partner services was apparently also involved, the impact on agency ‘business’ is all the greater.” The news broke in a week in which Germany’s intelligence service directors had testified to parliament about the heightened threat posed by powers including Russia and China. The BND chief, Martin Jäger, a former ambassador to Ukraine, warned of a possible violent conflict with Moscow, accusing the Kremlin of mounting a “shadow war” of hybrid and drone attacks. “We sincerely want to be Germany’s first line of defence,” he said. Jäger was reportedly already aware of Henning’s impending arrest at the time of his testimony, which came weeks after a foiled drone bomb attack that Berlin has blamed on Moscow . skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Russia does not appear to be the recipient of Hanning’s alleged activities, according to reports, at least not directly. Der Spiegel named Azerbaijan and China among the possible clients, claims not confirmed by authorities. Baku has denied involvement, although Hanning served on the board of the German-Azerbaijani Forum “fostering ties” with the authoritarian-run key energy transit country. View image in fullscreen Azerbaijan has been named by Der Spiegel as a possible recipient of Hanning’s alleged activities, though it has been denied by Baku. Photograph: Kym Illman/Getty Images Hanning’s primary motive may have been financial. He sat on the board of failed Latvian bank PNB Banka, which was declared insolvent in 2019. Bild newspaper said Hanning and another member of the supervisory board – reported to be the former Nato secretary general Anders Fogh Rasmussen – were held liable for up to €4m. Bild reported that Hanning’s pension had been confiscated to service the debt. The secret services are facing a reform drive long held back by sensitivities over abuses under the Nazi and communist dictatorships. A law due to pass parliament this year would lift many of the restraints imposed during the postwar period. Manns warned against any call to stop the measures in light of the Hanning case, saying it would “play into the hands of our opponents, who want a weak German foreign service”. Hanning was the face of German intelligence during a turbulent period of the post-cold war period, overseeing anti-terror strategy after the 9/11 attacks which were planned in part by a cell in Hamburg. Investigators only learned of his alleged criminal activities while gathering evidence in a separate child kidnapping case involving a steakhouse restaurant dynasty, which he is accused of abetting using his Israeli intelligence contacts. The treason charges have sparked a range of troubling questions. Were there other moles? How could his espionage have gone undetected so long? Was the classified information passed to third parties? And who will still trust Germany’s intelligence agencies? The charges against Hanning are hardly the first scandal to rock the country’s secret services in recent years, with high-profile cases involving spying for Russian intelligence and the CIA . More broadly, the former head of the domestic intelligence service, Hans-Georg Maaßen, has allied himself with hard-right groups and causes , raising doubts about the neutrality of the agency on his watch. And the former chancellor Gerhard Schröder, once a Social Democratic stalwart and respected economic reformer, has shocked Germans by taking on a string of lucrative Russian corporate jobs since leaving office in 2005 while becoming a close friend of Vladimir Putin , even attending the Kremlin strongman’s 74th birthday celebrations in Moscow this week. And with the far-right, pro-Russian party Alternative für Deutschland on the brink of power in a German state for the first time since the second world war, authorities are racing to restrict its access to sensitive intelligence . With criticism mounting of the legions of former senior German officials who cash in on work relating to their previous activities, Von Notz and Manns joined a chorus calling for a lifelong lobbying ban for high-ranking intelligence officers.
